title: 10. Exercises: Memory Management Masterclass (Part 2)
objectives: Solve the Memory Management Masterclass exercises without looking at the lesson
Test edge cases and explain your approach

sections.title: tracemalloc — Memory Profiling — Coding Challenges — Concept 21
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
tracemalloc basics:
  a) Start tracemalloc with 20-frame depth
  b) Allocate 5 different types of objects (list, dict, str, class, array)
  c) Take a snapshot and show top 10 allocations by lineno
  d) Show top 5 by filename
  e) Show top 3 with full traceback
  f) Display the source code line for each allocation site

CHALLENGE 2:
Snapshot comparison tool:
  Build a SnapshotComparator class:
  a) add_snapshot(label): takes and stores a snapshot
  b) compare(label1, label2): compares two named snapshots
  c) growth_report(label1, label2, top_n=10): shows top growth areas
  d) stable_check(label1, label2, threshold_kb=1): asserts no significant growth
  e) Test: allocate increasing amounts between snapshots
  f) Verify: stable_check fails on leaky code, passes on clean code

CHALLENGE 3:
Memory profiling decorator:
  Build @profile_memory(n_runs=10, warmup=3) decorator:
  a) Warmup: run function N times to stabilize caches
  b) Baseline: take snapshot
  c) Test runs: execute function N more times
  d) Final: take snapshot, compare
  e) Report: avg bytes per call, peak, top allocation sites
  f) Handle: nested calls (profiling a profiled function)
  g) Test with: sorted(), list comprehension, generator, numpy

CHALLENGE 4:
Production monitoring integration:
  Build a MemoryWatchdog class that:
  a) Runs in background thread, samples every 30 seconds
  b) Alerts (prints/logs) if memory grows > 10MB between samples
  c) On alert: captures full traceback snapshot, saves to file
  d) Provides REST-style interface: /memory/report endpoint
  e) Tracks: rolling 1-hour history of memory samples
  f) Auto-disables tracemalloc if overhead > 20% CPU
     (heuristic: compare time with/without)

CHALLENGE 5:
Allocation site optimizer:
  Given a function with high memory usage, use tracemalloc to:
  a) Identify the top 3 allocation sites
  b) Propose and implement an optimization for each
  c) Measure before and after for each optimization
  d) Calculate: total memory saved, performance impact
  Test function: a string processing pipeline with 1M strings

CHALLENGE 6:
tracemalloc filter builder:
  Build a FlexibleFilter class that creates tracemalloc filters:
  a) include_module(module_name): filter to specific module
  b) exclude_stdlib(): exclude all stdlib allocations
  c) min_size(bytes): only show allocations above threshold
  d) between_lines(file, start, end): focus on specific code region
  e) combine(*filters): AND/OR combination of filters
  f) apply(snapshot): returns filtered snapshot
  g) Test: reduce a noisy snapshot to only your application code

CHALLENGE 7:
Complete memory profiling report generator:
  Build a system that:
  a) Profiles a function at 3 scales (N=1K, 10K, 100K)
  b) Takes tracemalloc snapshots at each scale
  c) Identifies allocation patterns: O(n), O(n²), O(log n)
  d) Generates a detailed text/HTML report with:
     - Memory vs input size chart (text-based)
     - Top 10 allocation sites per scale
     - Predicted memory at N=1M
     - Specific recommendations
  e) Test on: list of dicts, pandas-like operations, string processing
```

sections.title: sys.getsizeof() — Object Size — Coding Challenges — Concept 22
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Complete size reference chart:
  Measure sys.getsizeof for 30 Python objects:
  - All basic types: None, bool, int (various sizes), float, complex
  - Strings: empty, 1 char, 10 chars, 100 chars, 1000 chars
  - Bytes: same sizes as strings
  - Containers: empty and 1/10/100 items: list, tuple, dict, set
  - Custom class with and without __slots__
  Present as a sorted table: object | size_bytes | notes

CHALLENGE 2:
True size calculator:
  Build true_sizeof(obj) that:
  a) Recursively measures total memory including all contents
  b) Handles cycles (use seen set of ids)
  c) Handles shared objects (count only once)
  d) Handles numpy arrays (use .nbytes)
  e) Returns breakdown: {type: total_bytes}
  f) Test with: nested dict, circular reference, shared sublist

CHALLENGE 3:
Data structure memory optimizer:
  Given a dataset of 1M records, find the most memory-efficient representation:
  a) List of dicts
  b) Dict of lists
  c) List of namedtuples
  d) List of dataclasses
  e) List of slotted dataclasses
  f) Numpy structured array
  g) Pandas DataFrame (if available)
  Measure true memory for each. Rank by efficiency.

CHALLENGE 4:
Memory budget enforcer:
  Build a @memory_budget(max_bytes) decorator:
  a) Before calling the function, record memory usage
  b) After calling, measure memory increase
  c) If increase > max_bytes, raise MemoryError with details
  d) Report: where memory was allocated (tracemalloc)
  e) Test with: functions that allocate small/medium/large amounts

CHALLENGE 5:
Collection overhead analyzer:
  For each Python collection type (list, dict, set, tuple, deque, array):
  a) Measure size at 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 items
  b) Calculate overhead per item
  c) Find the resize thresholds (where size jumps)
  d) Calculate wasted space at each size
  e) Recommend: which collection is most memory-efficient for each N?

CHALLENGE 6:
String memory analyzer:
  Investigate Python string memory:
  a) ASCII vs UTF-8 vs UTF-16 vs UTF-32 strings (4 kinds internally)
  b) Show: 'hello' vs 'héllo' vs '你好' use different bytes/char
  c) Measure: how string size grows with length
  d) Measure: interned vs non-interned strings
  e) Find: at what length does sys.intern() stop being worthwhile?
  f) Measure: f-string vs concatenation vs join memory

CHALLENGE 7:
Production object size auditor:
  Build an ObjectSizeAuditor class:
  a) audit(obj, label): records size breakdown for an object
  b) compare(label1, label2): compares two snapshots
  c) report_top(n=10): shows largest objects by true_sizeof
  d) find_duplicates(): finds objects with same value but multiple copies
     (using hash + equality) — suggests interning opportunities
  e) estimate_savings(obj): calculates memory that could be saved by:
     - Using __slots__
     - Interning repeated strings
     - Using array instead of list (for numeric data)
```

sections.title: Memory-Mapped Files (mmap) — Coding Challenges — Concept 23
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
mmap basics:
  a) Create a 1MB file with structured data (1000 records × 1KB each)
  b) Memory-map it with read/write access
  c) Read record 500 without reading records 1-499
  d) Modify record 500 in-place
  e) Verify: file on disk reflects the change
  f) Measure: time to access random record vs seek()

CHALLENGE 2:
Binary search on mmap:
  a) Create a sorted binary file (1M int64 values, 8 bytes each)
  b) Implement binary search using mmap (no loading to list!)
  c) Find 1000 random values in the sorted file
  d) Compare: mmap binary search vs load-all-then-search
  e) Measure: time and memory for each approach

CHALLENGE 3:
mmap-based key-value store:
  Build a simple persistent key-value store using mmap:
  a) File format: [header: 4KB][index: 1MB][data: remaining]
  b) put(key, value): store key-value pair
  c) get(key): retrieve value by key
  d) delete(key): mark as deleted (tombstone)
  e) Persist to disk automatically (mmap + flush)
  f) Load existing store from file on startup

CHALLENGE 4:
Multi-process shared memory:
  Using mmap for IPC:
  a) Create anonymous mmap before fork()
  b) Producer process: write 1000 values to shared memory
  c) Consumer process: read values from shared memory
  d) Add a semaphore (using mmap!) to synchronize
  e) Verify: data shared correctly, no race conditions
  f) Measure: mmap IPC vs multiprocessing.Queue speed

CHALLENGE 5:
Large file word counter:
  Count word frequencies in a 1GB text file using mmap:
  a) Create a 1GB test file (repeated Lorem Ipsum)
  b) mmap approach: iterate through mmap finding word boundaries
  c) Chunked approach: read in 64MB chunks
  d) Normal approach: read entire file (if RAM allows)
  e) Measure: time, peak RAM, throughput for each
  f) Find: at what file size does mmap become necessary?

CHALLENGE 6:
mmap ring buffer:
  Implement a lock-free ring buffer using mmap:
  a) Fixed-size circular buffer backed by mmap
  b) Producer: write items to ring buffer
  c) Consumer: read items from ring buffer
  d) Works across processes (using file-backed mmap)
  e) Uses atomic operations for head/tail pointers (struct module)
  f) Benchmark: throughput vs multiprocessing.Queue

CHALLENGE 7:
Memory-mapped database index:
  Build a B-tree-like index on an mmap file:
  a) Index maps integer keys to file offsets
  b) Backed by mmap — survives process restart
  c) insert(key, offset): add to index
  d) lookup(key): find offset for key
  e) range_query(lo, hi): find all keys in range
  f) Test with: 1M entries, random inserts and lookups
  g) Compare: mmap index vs in-memory dict performance
```

sections.title: array Module & NumPy for Memory Efficiency — Coding Challenges — Concept 24
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
array module mastery:
  a) Create arrays of all 12 type codes
  b) Measure itemsize and total size for 1M items each
  c) Show: type code selection saves memory
  d) Binary file I/O: write array to file, read back (array.tofile/fromfile)
  e) Verify: binary file size = N * itemsize (no Python overhead!)
  f) Benchmark: read 1M int32 values from file via array vs struct loop

CHALLENGE 2:
Memory optimizer for real data:
  Given a dataset of 1M records:
  {'user_id': int, 'age': int, 'score': float, 'active': bool}
  a) Measure memory as list of dicts
  b) Measure as dict of lists (column-oriented)
  c) Measure as dict of arrays (array.array per column)
  d) Measure as numpy structured array
  e) Recommend the best structure with justification

CHALLENGE 3:
NumPy view vs copy benchmark:
  a) Create a 1GB float64 array
  b) Test 10 operations that create VIEWS (no extra memory)
  c) Test 10 operations that create COPIES (extra memory)
  d) Measure memory for each
  e) Find unexpected copies (operations you thought were views)
  f) Build a cheat sheet: which numpy operations are views?

CHALLENGE 4:
Dtype optimization for ML:
  Given a neural network weight matrix (1000×1000 float64):
  a) Try float64 (baseline)
  b) Try float32 (standard ML)
  c) Try float16 (half precision)
  d) Measure: memory for each
  e) Measure: computation speed for matrix multiply
  f) Measure: precision loss (max absolute error vs float64)
  g) Recommend: when to use each dtype in production ML

CHALLENGE 5:
array-based ring buffer:
  Implement a fixed-size circular buffer using array.array:
  a) Fixed capacity set at creation
  b) push(value): add value, overwrite oldest if full
  c) pop(): remove and return oldest value
  d) peek(): read without removing
  e) is_full(), is_empty(), __len__()
  f) Compare memory: array ring buffer vs list ring buffer vs deque
  g) Benchmark: 1M push/pop operations for each

CHALLENGE 6:
NumPy memory layout optimizer:
  For a 2D array of shape (1000, 1000):
  a) C-order (row-major) vs Fortran-order (column-major)
  b) Measure row-access speed for each
  c) Measure column-access speed for each
  d) Show cache efficiency difference (big performance impact!)
  e) For a specific algorithm (matrix multiply), find optimal order
  f) Use np.ascontiguousarray() / np.asfortranarray() to convert
  g) Measure memory overhead of conversion

CHALLENGE 7:
Production numeric data pipeline:
  Build a pipeline that processes 1B sensor readings efficiently:
  a) Generate: 1B readings as Python generator (can't fit in RAM)
  b) Chunk: process in 1M-item numpy chunks
  c) Downsample: convert float64 to float32 (halve memory)
  d) Aggregate: compute rolling statistics without materializing all data
  e) Store: efficient binary format (array.tofile or numpy.save)
  f) Load: read back and verify with numpy.load
  g) Compare: total time and peak memory vs naive list approach
```
